facts.title: SK hynix Unveils First HBF Standard Specifications with SanDisk at FMS 2026
facts.event_hint: SK hynix and SanDisk released the first open standard specifications for High Bandwidth Flash (HBF) via OCP, announced at FMS 2026 (Santa Clara, Aug 4-6, 2026); HBF is positioned as a new memory layer between HBM and SSDs for AI inference.
facts.problem: AI inference is driving a surge in data volumes to process, creating simultaneous memory-bandwidth and capacity-scalability bottlenecks that existing HBM (high bandwidth, limited capacity) and SSD (high capacity, lower bandwidth) layers each only partially address.
facts.mechanism: High Bandwidth Flash (HBF) is positioned as a new memory layer between HBM and SSDs: it leverages NAND die stacking to deliver HBM-like high-speed data transfer while significantly expanding capacity beyond what HBM provides. The standard adopts the UCIe industry-standard die-to-die interconnect so HBF can integrate across processor types (GPUs, CPUs), and it defines connection interfaces/electrical characteristics, reliability and packaging guidelines for the HBF die-stack process, and software I/O guidelines. The specification was published as an open standard through the Open Compute Project (OCP).

evidence.claim: HBF capacity specifications cover up to 512GB, based on two stack configurations (8-high and 16-high NAND dies).
evidence.condition: Announced standard specification (8-high / 16-high NAND die stacks); not a measured shipping device
evidence.source_locator: Spec paragraph: 'Capacity specifications cover up to 512GB based on two stack configurations (8-high and 16-high NAND dies)'

evidence.claim: HBF bandwidth is categorized into three grades (Grade1-3), delivering scalable performance from approximately 0.4TB/s to 3.0TB/s.
evidence.condition: Announced standard specification across Grade1~3; spec target, not an independent measured result
evidence.source_locator: Spec paragraph: 'Bandwidth is categorized into three grades (Grade1~3), delivering scalable performance from approximately 0.4TB/s to 3.0TB/s'

evidence.claim: HBF adopts the UCIe industry-standard interconnect, laying the groundwork to integrate HBF across different processor types including GPUs and CPUs.
evidence.condition: Standard specification; processor-portability is a stated design intent
evidence.source_locator: Interconnect paragraph: 'HBF technology adopts UCIe ... to flexibly integrate ... across different processor types, including GPUs and CPUs'

evidence.claim: HBF is positioned as a new memory layer between HBM and SSDs, enabling high-speed data transfer similar to HBM while significantly expanding capacity by leveraging NAND technology, targeting AI inference bandwidth and capacity bottlenecks.
evidence.condition: Vendor positioning statement; no quantitative HBM-vs-HBF comparison visible in the evidence pack
evidence.source_locator: HBF technology paragraph: 'a new memory layer between HBM and SSDs ... high-speed data transfer similar to HBM while significantly expanding capacity by leveraging NAND technology'

evidence.claim: The HBF standard was disclosed as an open standard through the Open Compute Project (OCP); the consortium launched ~February 2026 after the initial SK hynix-SanDisk standardization partnership in August 2025, with Google and Tenstorrent currently participating.
evidence.condition: Open standard via OCP; consortium status as of Aug 4, 2026 announcement
evidence.source_locator: OCP/consortium paragraphs: 'disclosed through the Open Compute Project (OCP) ... about six months after launching the consortium in February ... Google and Tenstorrent currently participating'

facts.evaluation_context: This is a vendor product/standardization announcement (SK hynix newsroom), not an experimental or system-evaluation paper. No measured benchmarks, no real-workload results, no independent validation in the evidence. Visible quantitative specs: capacity up to 512GB (8-high/16-high NAND stacks); bandwidth ~0.4-3.0 TB/s across three grades; UCIe interconnect. Venue: FMS 2026, Santa Clara Convention Center, Aug 4-6, 2026. Standardization timeline: SK hynix-SanDisk partnership Aug 2025, consortium launch Feb 2026, spec unveiling Aug 4, 2026.
facts.limitations: The announcement discloses standard specifications, not a mass-produced, sampled, or deployed product; per the project-context card, announced specs must be distinguished from sampling, mass production, and scale deployment, and these spec numbers should not be read as measured device capabilities. The evidence pack contains no access latency, P/E endurance, write amplification, power draw, cost/bit, or system-level / real-workload performance data. Headline comparative claims referenced in discovery (roughly 2.5x power-efficiency gain over a prior generation and ~540x capacity vs HBM) are NOT present in the visible Evidence Pack and are therefore not recorded as facts. No independent third-party validation; the source is a vendor newsroom/marketing release.
facts.project_relevance: HBF directly addresses the storage-media topic's question of whether a new non-volatile medium can shift the AI memory hierarchy boundary: it is an OCP open standard for a NAND-stacked, UCIe-interfaced layer sitting between HBM and SSDs, with concrete capacity (up to 512GB) and bandwidth (0.4-3.0 TB/s) specs. It is relevant to judging whether media innovation is moving from device metrics toward system usability, but the visible evidence only reaches the announced-standard stage, not measured system value. For the project, the open-standard + UCIe + multi-vendor-consortium framing (SK hynix, SanDisk, Google, Tenstorrent) is a deployment-ecosystem signal worth tracking, while power, endurance, latency, cost, and a clear mass-production timeline remain the gating unknowns. (Project inference, separate from source facts.)
source_notes: Evidence pack is the front ~46% of the source (3503 of 7581 chars, 0.5379 reduction), so additional quantitative claims may exist in the unread portion.
Discovery summary referenced a ~2.5x power-efficiency improvement and ~540x capacity vs HBM; these are not visible in the Evidence Pack and are recorded as evidence_gaps rather than facts.

facts.title: Kioxia and SanDisk 10th-Gen 332-Layer QLC NAND Achieves Industry's Highest Bit Density
facts.event_hint: Kioxia and SanDisk unveil 10th-generation 332-layer QLC 3D flash memory technology at FMS 2026 (Aug 4, 2026), claiming industry-highest QLC bit density.
facts.problem: AI training, inference, and hyperscale datacenter workloads are driving rapid data growth, pressuring storage to deliver higher capacity density, interface bandwidth, and power efficiency simultaneously within fixed power/cooling envelopes.
facts.mechanism: CMOS directly Bonded to Array (CBA) architecture fabricates CMOS logic and the memory array on separate wafers, then bonds them with high-precision wafer-to-wafer alignment; combined with a 332-layer optimized floorplan, Toggle DDR6.0 interface with Separate Command Address (SCA) protocol, and Power-Isolated Low-Tapped Termination (PI-LTT) for I/O data-out transfer power efficiency.

evidence.claim: 332-layer QLC 3D flash delivers up to 60% increase in bit density versus 8th-generation, achieving >37 Gb/mm^2.
evidence.condition: Vendor-stated spec from joint press release; QLC, 332-layer architecture with optimized floorplan.
evidence.source_locator: Section 'Key 10th-generation QLC 3D flash memory technology highlights' (first bullet); also stated in lead press release paragraph.

evidence.claim: First QLC 3D flash memory technology to reach a 4.8 Gb/s NAND interface, enabled by Toggle DDR6.0 and the Separate Command Address (SCA) protocol.
evidence.baseline: 8th-generation 3D flash memory (read/write bandwidth improved relative to it)
evidence.condition: 1 Gb/s calculated as 1,000,000,000 bits/s; value obtained under Kioxia/SanDisk specific test environment and may vary depending on use conditions.
evidence.source_locator: Section 'Key 10th-generation QLC 3D flash memory technology highlights' (second bullet); footnote 3 on 4.8 Gb/s test condition.

evidence.claim: CBA (CMOS directly Bonded to Array) architecture enhances density scaling, performance, and manufacturing efficiency.
evidence.condition: Each CMOS wafer and cell array wafer manufactured separately in optimized condition then bonded (footnote 2).
evidence.source_locator: Section 'Key 10th-generation QLC 3D flash memory technology highlights' (third bullet); footnote 2.

evidence.claim: PI-LTT (Power-Isolated Low-Tapped Termination) improves I/O data-out transfer power efficiency, addressing AI/cloud power and cooling challenges.
evidence.condition: No quantified percentage or absolute power figure given in the evidence.
evidence.source_locator: Section 'Key 10th-generation QLC 3D flash memory technology highlights' (fourth bullet); lead paragraph on power efficiency.

evidence.claim: Industry's highest bit density for QLC NAND benchmark, based on Kioxia and Sandisk survey as of August 3, 2026.
evidence.baseline: Industry QLC NAND (self-survey by Kioxia and Sandisk)
evidence.condition: Self-reported vendor survey, not an independent benchmark; 'benchmark 1' / 'industry's first' / 'industry's highest' are vendor claims.
evidence.source_locator: Lead paragraph ('setting the industry benchmark 1'); footnote 'As of August 3, 2026, based on Kioxia and Sandisk survey.'

facts.evaluation_context: Press-release technology announcement (not a benchmarked product). No workload, SSD-level throughput, latency, P/E endurance, write amplification, random I/O, absolute power draw, or cost/bit disclosed. Comparisons are to the companies' own 8th-generation; the 4.8 Gb/s interface figure is measured under an unspecified vendor test environment. Stage: unveiled at Future of Memory and Storage (FMS) 2026; Kioxia states it will 'accelerate development toward the commercialization' of 10th-gen QLC products.
facts.limitations: This is a vendor press release announcing technology, not a shipping product; no mass-production or sampling date, no device-level endurance (P/E cycles), no latency, no random bandwidth, no absolute power consumption, and no cost/bit are provided. All 'industry first/highest' claims rest on a Kioxia-SanDisk self-survey (as of Aug 3, 2026), not independent testing. The 4.8 Gb/s interface speed is explicitly noted to vary with use conditions. Read/write bandwidth improvement over 8th-gen is asserted but not quantified.
facts.project_relevance: Directly relevant to the NAND/Flash density-vs-system-value question: concrete generational density (>37 Gb/mm^2, +60%) and interface (4.8 Gb/s) gains are now claimed at the die level, but the evidence stops short of system-level metrics (endurance, latency, random I/O, absolute power, cost/bit, deployment timeline) needed to judge whether this moves QLC into a new tier of the AI storage hierarchy. Treat as a vendor roadmap/announce signal, not a deployable capability, pending commercialization and independent SSD/system benchmarks.
source_notes: Primary source is a Kioxia/SanDisk joint press release (vendor source level A, but marketing/announcement content).
Evidence pack is the vendor press release; no peer-reviewed or independent benchmark data present.

evidence_gaps.question: What is the P/E endurance (program-erase cycles) and write amplification of the 10th-gen 332-layer QLC, which determines deployability for write-intensive AI workloads?
What is the quantified power-efficiency improvement (percentage or absolute mW/Gb/s) that PI-LTT and the interface enhancements deliver, since the press release claims large gains without a number?
What is the mass-production / sampling timeline and target SSD capacity for the 10th-gen QLC products, given only an intent to 'accelerate development toward commercialization'?
